unit.title: Lumped elements and the brute-force method
unit.intro:
Model a circuit as ideal elements connected by wires, describe each element by its
v–i relation, and see how KCL and KVL give exactly enough equations to solve any circuit.

steps.title: The lumped element abstraction
steps.md:
In 6.200 we model real circuits as **lumped elements**: ideal two-terminal parts connected by
perfect wires. Each element is completely described by one relation between the voltage across
it and the current through it, its **constitutive relation**:

| element | constitutive relation |
|---|---|
| resistor $R$ | $v = R\,i$ |
| voltage source | $v = V$ (any current) |
| current source | $i = I$ (any voltage) |

Every element (or **branch**) has two unknowns: its voltage $v$ and its current $i$.

**Sign convention.** We always define the current as flowing *into the + end* of the element's
voltage. With that convention, $p = v \cdot i$ is the power **into** (absorbed by) the element.
A negative $p$ means the element is supplying power to the rest of the circuit.

steps.title: When is the lumped model allowed?
steps.md:
Real wires and parts are made of distributed charge and fields, so treating them as ideal "lumps" is
an approximation. It is valid when three things hold:

1. **No net charge piles up inside an element.** Whatever current enters one terminal leaves the
   other, so the element has *one* current.
2. **No changing magnetic flux links the space outside the elements.** Then the voltage between
   two points doesn't depend on the path you take between them, so each element has *one* voltage.
3. **The circuit is small compared with the wavelength** of its signals, $\lambda = c/f$. Signals then
   reach every part of the circuit essentially at once, and nothing travels like a wave down the wires.

> **Intuition:** at 60 Hz the wavelength is about 5000 km, so any circuit on a desk is tiny by comparison.
> At a few GHz (Wi-Fi, phone radios) the wavelength is a few centimeters, the size of a circuit
> board itself. That's where lumped analysis starts to fail and engineers switch to transmission-line models.

The payoff of these assumptions is huge. Instead of Maxwell's equations, you only need algebra
between voltages and currents.

q.name: A0
q.prompt: Roughly what is the wavelength of a 1 GHz signal? (Use $c = 3\times10^8$ m/s.)
q.why: $\lambda = c/f = 3\times10^8 / 10^9 = 0.3$ m. A 30 cm circuit is no longer small compared with that, so the lumped model would be questionable.

steps.title: Using the sign convention
steps.md:
The **associated reference directions** (current into +) are a bookkeeping rule. You may pick the
direction of either label however you like; the math tells you the truth through signs.

* If you guess a current's direction wrong, the answer simply comes out negative. That is not an error.
* What you *must* do is be consistent: once $v$ and $i$ are labeled, $p = vi$ is the absorbed power
  only if $i$ enters the + end. If your current label points into the − end, the absorbed power is $-vi$.

**Conservation check.** In any circuit, the absorbed powers of all elements add up to exactly zero
(Tellegen's theorem). Whatever the sources supply, the other elements absorb. This is a great way to
check a finished solution.

> **Watch out:** a source is not *always* a supplier. Charging a battery means the battery absorbs power,
> because current is pushed *into* its + terminal.

q.name: A1
q.prompt: A branch has a voltage of 3 V and a current of −2 A, defined into its + end. How much power does it absorb?
q.why: $p = v\,i = (3\text{ V})(-2\text{ A}) = -6\text{ W}$. Negative absorbed power means the element delivers 6 W to the rest of the circuit.

steps.title: Kirchhoff's laws
steps.md:
Two laws tie the elements together.

* **KCL** (conservation of charge): at every node, the currents leaving sum to zero,
  $\sum_j i_j = 0$. Add all currents with the same direction relative to the node.
* **KVL** (from Faraday's law): around every closed loop, the branch voltages sum to zero,
  $\sum_k v_k = 0$. Add voltages with the same polarity as you walk around the loop. The signs
  matter.

For a circuit with $B$ branches and $N$ nodes:

* $B$ constitutive equations (one per element),
* $N - 1$ independent KCL equations (the last node's equation is implied by the others),
* $B - N + 1$ independent KVL equations.

That is $2B$ equations for the $2B$ unknowns, so the circuit can always be solved.

steps.title: Why those counts?
steps.md:
**Why only $N-1$ KCL equations?** Every branch current leaves one node and enters another, so it
appears in exactly two KCL equations, once with each sign. Add up all $N$ node equations and every
current cancels, giving $0 = 0$. So any one of them is the negative sum of the others and adds no new
information. Throw one away, conventionally at the node you'll call ground.

**Why $B - N + 1$ KVL equations?** Draw a *tree*, a set of branches that connects all $N$ nodes without
forming a loop. A tree always has exactly $N - 1$ branches. Each of the remaining $B - N + 1$ branches
closes exactly one new loop, and each of those loops gives one independent KVL equation. For a flat
drawing this is the same as counting the "windows" of the picture.

> **Intuition:** think of potential as height. KVL says that if you walk around any loop and come back to
> where you started, your total climb is zero. KCL is like water in pipes: what flows into a junction must
> flow out, because water (charge) doesn't pile up there.

q.name: A2
q.prompt: A circuit has 5 branches and 4 nodes. How many independent KCL equations does it have?

q.name: A3
q.prompt: For that same circuit (5 branches, 4 nodes), how many independent KVL equations are there?
q.why: $B - N + 1 = 5 - 4 + 1 = 2$. For a planar circuit, one per smallest enclosed loop (each "window" of the drawing).

steps.title: The brute-force method, worked through
steps.md: Label every branch with a voltage and a current (directions are arbitrary, but each current points into its element's + end). Then write all $2B = 10$ equations. **Constitutive:** $v_1 = 5$ V, $v_2 = 4\Omega \cdot i_2$, $v_3 = 2\Omega \cdot i_3$, $i_4 = -2$ A (the source pushes 2 A upward, against the downward current label), $v_5 = 3\Omega \cdot i_5$. Notice there is *no* equation for $v_4$: a current source doesn't constrain its own voltage. **KCL** (3 nodes): $i_1 + i_2 = 0$, $i_2 = i_3 + i_5$, $i_3 = i_4$. **KVL** (2 windows): $v_1 = v_2 + v_3 + v_4$ (left), $v_4 + v_3 = v_5$ (right). Solving the 10 equations gives, for example, $v_5 = \frac{39}{7}\,\text{V} \approx 5.571\,\text{V}$ and $v_4 = \frac{67}{7}\,\text{V} \approx 9.571\,\text{V}$. This always works, but 10 equations for a 5-element circuit is a lot. The next lecture's **node method** needs only one equation here.

steps.title: Checking the example's power balance
steps.md:
With everything solved you can check the answer with power conservation. Using current into +:

* The 5 V source carries $i_1 = -i_2 = \frac{1}{7}\,\text{A} \approx 0.1429\,\text{A}$ into its + end, so it absorbs
  $5\,i_1 = \frac{5}{7}\,\text{W} \approx 0.7143\,\text{W}$. It's positive: the current source is strong enough to push
  current backwards into the voltage source, which is *absorbing* power (like a battery being charged).
* The resistors absorb $i^2 R$: the 4 Ω absorbs $\frac{4}{49}\,\text{W} \approx 0.08163\,\text{W}$, the 2 Ω absorbs 8 W,
  and the 3 Ω absorbs $\frac{507}{49}\,\text{W} \approx 10.35\,\text{W}$.
* The current source has $v_4 = 67/7$ V across it and pushes 2 A *out of* its + end, so it absorbs
  $-2 \cdot 67/7 = -134/7$ W. It is the only element supplying power.

Add all five and you get exactly zero, which confirms the solution.

> **Watch out:** the most common brute-force mistakes are sign slips in KVL (going *up* across a
> resistor when your label says *down*) and forgetting that a current source sets the current but not
> the voltage. When signs are confusing, redraw each element with its + and − marked before writing anything.

q.name: A4
q.prompt: In the example, $v_5 = 39/7$ V across the 3 Ω resistor. What is $i_5$?
q.why: Ohm's law: $i_5 = v_5 / 3\Omega = \frac{39/7}{3} = \frac{13}{7}$ A.

options: A current source fixes its current, not its voltage; the rest of the circuit sets $v_4$
Because the 2 Ω resistor in series sets it to $2\Omega \times 2$ A
q.soln: A current source fixes its current, not its voltage; the rest of the circuit sets $v_4$
q.name: A5
q.prompt: Why is there no constitutive equation for $v_4$, the voltage across the 2 A source?
q.why: An ideal current source supplies its current at whatever voltage the circuit requires. $v_4$ comes out of the KVL equations ($v_4 = 67/7$ V here).

q.name: Q1
q.prompt: Quiz: with $v_1 = 5$ V, $v_3 = -4$ V and $v_4 = 67/7$ V, use the left-loop KVL equation $v_1 = v_2 + v_3 + v_4$ to find $v_2$.

q.name: Q2
q.prompt: Quiz: four currents leave a node: 2 A, −3 A, 0.5 A and $i$. What is $i$?

q.name: Q3
q.prompt: Quiz: a 2 Ω resistor carries 3 A. How much power does it absorb?
q.why: $p = v i = (R i) i = i^2 R = 9 \cdot 2 = 18$ W. Resistors always absorb power.

unit.title: Node analysis
unit.intro:
The brute-force method needs 2B equations. The node method organizes KCL so that only the
node potentials are unknown, which usually leaves just one or two equations.

steps.title: Why we need a better method
steps.md:
A circuit with $B$ branches has $2B$ unknowns (a voltage and a current per branch). Even a small
bridge of five resistors and a source has $B = 6$ and **12 unknowns**. We want a method that

* always works, and
* keeps the number of simultaneous equations small.

The idea: instead of solving for every branch voltage, solve for the **potential of each node**.
Once you know every node potential, every branch voltage is a difference of two of them, and
every current follows from the element laws.

steps.title: The node method, step by step
steps.md:
1. **Pick a reference node** (ground) and define its potential to be 0 V. A node that touches many
   elements, or one end of a voltage source, is a good choice.
2. **Label the potential** $e_k$ of every other node. These $N-1$ potentials are the unknowns.
   A voltage source tied to ground fixes its node's potential, so that one is already known.
3. **Write KCL at each unknown node**, putting each element law directly into the KCL sum. For a
   resistor between nodes $a$ and $b$, the current leaving $a$ is $(e_a - e_b)/R = G\,(e_a - e_b)$,
   where $G = 1/R$ is the **conductance**.
4. **Solve** the equations for the node potentials.
5. **Back-solve** for any branch voltage or current you need.

You only need $N-1$ equations (fewer if voltage sources fix some nodes), compared with $2B$ for
brute force.

steps.title: Where did KVL go?
steps.md:
The node method never writes a KVL equation, yet the answers satisfy KVL. Here is why. Every branch
voltage is written as a difference of node potentials, $v = e_a - e_b$. Walk around any loop and add
the branch voltages: each potential appears once with $+$ and once with $-$, so the sum **telescopes to
zero automatically**.

So choosing node potentials as unknowns builds KVL in for free. The element laws are substituted
directly, which leaves only KCL to write. That is why the count drops from $2B$ to $N-1$.

> **Intuition:** a node potential is like the altitude of a spot on a map. Once every spot has an altitude,
> "the total climb around a closed walk is zero" is automatically true. You never have to check it.

**What does "ground" mean here?** The reference node is just the zero of the potential scale, like
measuring altitude from sea level. Picking a different reference shifts every potential by the same
constant but changes no voltage *across* any element, and no current.

options: Writing every branch voltage as a difference of node potentials makes every loop sum cancel automatically
Because KVL doesn't apply to resistor circuits
Because the reference node absorbs any KVL error
q.soln: Writing every branch voltage as a difference of node potentials makes every loop sum cancel automatically
q.name: A1b
q.prompt: Why does node analysis never need a separate KVL equation?
q.why: Around a loop, $(e_a - e_b) + (e_b - e_c) + \dots + (e_z - e_a) = 0$ identically.

q.name: A1
q.prompt: A circuit has 6 nodes. One node is the reference, and a grounded voltage source fixes another node's potential. How many unknown node potentials remain?
q.why: $N - 1 = 5$ non-reference nodes, minus the one fixed by the source, leaves 4 unknowns.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.md: Ground the bottom node. The source fixes $e_3 = 12$ V, so the unknowns are $e_1$ and $e_2$. Write KCL as *currents leaving the node sum to zero*: $$e_1:\quad G_1(e_1 - 12) + G_2\,e_1 + G_3(e_1 - e_2) = 0$$ $$e_2:\quad G_3(e_2 - e_1) + G_4(e_2 - 12) + G_5\,e_2 - 1\text{ A} = 0$$ (the 1 A source pushes current *into* $e_2$, so it counts as $-1$ A leaving). Collect terms into matrix form $\mathbf{G}\,\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{i}$: $$\begin{bmatrix} G_1+G_2+G_3 & -G_3 \\ -G_3 & G_3+G_4+G_5 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} e_1 \\ e_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 12\,G_1 \\ 12\,G_4 + 1 \end{bmatrix}$$ Notice the pattern: each diagonal entry is the total conductance touching that node, and each off-diagonal entry is minus the conductance connecting the two nodes.

steps.title: Writing the matrix by inspection
steps.md:
For circuits of resistors and current sources, you can write $\mathbf{G}\,\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{i}$ without
any algebra:

* **Diagonal** $G_{kk}$: the sum of all conductances connected to node $k$ (including those to known
  nodes and to ground).
* **Off-diagonal** $G_{jk}$: minus the conductance directly between nodes $j$ and $k$ (0 if none).
  So $\mathbf{G}$ is always **symmetric**.
* **Right side** $i_k$: the source current pushed *into* node $k$, plus $G \cdot V$ for every resistor
  that connects node $k$ to a node whose potential $V$ is already known.

**Quick sanity checks before you solve:**

1. Every diagonal entry is positive and at least as large as the magnitudes of the other entries
   in its row. If not, you've dropped a term.
2. The matrix is symmetric. If $G_{12} \ne G_{21}$, there's a mistake (until dependent sources show up, which can break symmetry).
3. Units: $\mathbf{G}$ is in siemens, $\mathbf{i}$ in amperes, so $\mathbf{e}$ comes out in volts.

> **Watch out:** pick *one* convention for each KCL equation, either "sum of currents leaving = 0" or
> "currents in = currents out", and stick to it. Most sign errors come from mixing the two halfway through
> an equation. A current source pointing *into* the node counts as $-I$ in "leaving" form.

q.name: A2
q.prompt: With $G_1 = G_2 = \tfrac12$ S and $G_3 = 1$ S, what is the top-left entry $G_1 + G_2 + G_3$ of the matrix (in siemens)?
q.why: $\tfrac12 + \tfrac12 + 1 = 2$ S: the total conductance touching node $e_1$.

q.name: A3
q.prompt: Solve the two equations. What is $e_1$?
q.why: The matrix is $\begin{bmatrix}2 & -1\\ -1 & 1.5\end{bmatrix}$ with right side $\begin{bmatrix}6\\ 4\end{bmatrix}$. Its determinant is $2(1.5) - 1 = 2$, so $e_1 = \frac{1.5 \cdot 6 + 1 \cdot 4}{2} = 6.5$ V and $e_2 = \frac{2 \cdot 4 + 6}{2} = 7$ V.

q.name: A4
q.prompt: Back-solve: with $e_1 = 6.5$ V and $e_2 = 7$ V, what current flows through $R_3$ from $e_1$ to $e_2$?
q.why: $i = (e_1 - e_2)/R_3 = (6.5 - 7)/1 = -0.5$ A. The minus sign means 0.5 A actually flows from $e_2$ to $e_1$.

steps.title: Does the answer make sense?
steps.md:
After solving, look at the numbers before moving on.

* With **only one voltage source** and resistors, every node potential lies between 0 and that
  source's voltage. Resistors can only divide a voltage, never amplify it.
* Here $e_2 = 7$ V is *higher* than $e_1 = 6.5$ V even though $e_1$ is closer to the source in the
  drawing. That's because the 1 A current source pumps extra current into $e_2$, raising it. So
  current flows through $R_3$ from $e_2$ to $e_1$, and $i_3$ comes out negative.
* Check KCL at one node with the numbers: at $e_2$, the currents leaving are
  $(7 - 6.5)/1 + (7 - 12)/4 + 7/4 = 0.5 - 1.25 + 1.75 = 1$ A, which is exactly what the source pushes in. ✓

> **Intuition:** a current source "pushes" current into a node, like a pump pushing water into a tank, so
> the node's potential rises until the resistors can carry that current away.

options: It is one end of the voltage source, so the other end's potential is known immediately
The reference must always be the node at the bottom of the drawing
It has the fewest elements connected to it
q.soln: It is one end of the voltage source, so the other end's potential is known immediately
q.name: A5
q.prompt: Why is the bottom node a good reference in this example?
q.why: Any node can be the reference, and the answers for voltages *across* elements don't change. Grounding one side of a voltage source removes an unknown for free.

q.name: Q1
q.prompt: Quiz: find the node potential $e$.
q.why: KCL at $e$ (currents leaving): $\frac{e - 10}{5} + \frac{e}{20} - 1 = 0$, so $e\left(\frac15 + \frac1{20}\right) = 3$ and $e = 12$ V.

q.name: Q2
q.prompt: Quiz: in the same circuit, what current flows through the 5 Ω resistor from the source toward node $e$?
q.why: $(10 - 12)/5 = -0.4$ A: current actually flows from $e$ back into the source. The 1 A source supplies it.

q.name: Q3
q.prompt: Quiz: a circuit of only resistors and current sources has 7 nodes. How many node equations do you need to solve?
q.why: $N - 1 = 6$: one KCL equation per non-reference node.

unit.title: Supernodes and series/parallel combinations
unit.intro:
Handle voltage sources that float between two unknown nodes, and simplify circuits by
combining resistors in series and in parallel before you write any equations.

steps.title: The problem with floating voltage sources
steps.md: Here $V_B$ sits between two **non-reference** nodes. Try writing KCL at $e_1$: you need the current through $V_B$, but a voltage source's current can be anything. It isn't set by $e_1$ and $e_2$, so you can't write it in terms of node potentials.

options: The current through an ideal voltage source is not determined by its voltage
KCL does not apply at nodes that touch a voltage source
q.soln: The current through an ideal voltage source is not determined by its voltage
q.name: A1
q.prompt: Why can't you write an ordinary KCL equation at $e_1$ in terms of node potentials?
q.why: A voltage source fixes $v$, never $i$. So its current has no element law to substitute into KCL.

steps.title: Supernodes
steps.md:
The fix trades the two lost KCL equations for two new ones.

1. **The source relation (KVL):** the source fixes the *difference* of the two potentials,
   $e_1 - e_2 = V_B$.
2. **Supernode KCL:** draw a closed surface around both nodes and the source (a *supernode*).
   Charge is conserved for any closed surface, not just a single node, so the currents leaving
   the surface sum to zero. The source's own current stays inside, so it never appears:

$$\frac{e_1 - V_A}{R_1} + \frac{e_1}{R_2} + \frac{e_2}{R_3} = 0$$

That is two equations for the two unknowns. Each floating source removes two ordinary KCL
equations and gives back exactly two.

steps.title: Supernodes in practice
steps.md:
**A recipe:**

1. Circle each floating voltage source together with the two nodes it connects. If several voltage
   sources are chained together, one supernode can swallow all of them.
2. Write one **constraint** per source: $e_+ - e_- = V$ (+ terminal minus − terminal).
3. Write **one KCL** for the whole supernode, summing every current that crosses the circle. Currents
   between nodes *inside* the circle never appear.
4. Write ordinary KCL at every other unknown node.

**Can you avoid supernodes?** Often, yes. If a circuit has only one voltage source, make one of its
terminals the reference. Then the other terminal's potential is simply known. Supernodes are only
unavoidable when there are several voltage sources that don't share a node.

> **Intuition:** the source holds its two nodes a fixed distance apart in potential, like a rigid rod
> joining them. They move together, so effectively there is only one unknown (where the rod sits),
> and one balance equation (total current out of the pair) to find it.

> **Watch out:** a voltage source in **series with a resistor** between two nodes is *not* a supernode
> problem. The resistor sets the current, $(e_a - V - e_b)/R$, so ordinary KCL works fine.

q.name: A2
q.prompt: Solve the supernode equations ($V_A = 10$ V, $R_1 = 2$ Ω, $R_2 = R_3 = 4$ Ω, $V_B = 3$ V). What is $e_1$?
q.why: Multiply the supernode KCL by 4: $2(e_1 - 10) + e_1 + e_2 = 0$, so $3e_1 + e_2 = 20$. Substitute $e_2 = e_1 - 3$: $4e_1 = 23$, so $e_1 = 5.75$ V.

q.name: A3
q.prompt: What current flows through $V_B$, from $e_1$ to $e_2$?
q.why: Everything that leaves through $V_B$ must continue down through $R_3$: $i = e_2/R_3 = 2.75/4 = 11/16$ A.

steps.title: Series and parallel resistors
steps.md:
**Series:** elements are in series when they carry the *same current*. Their voltages add, so
$$R_\text{series} = R_1 + R_2 + \dots + R_N.$$

**Parallel:** elements are in parallel when they share the *same two nodes*, and therefore the same
voltage. Their currents add, so their conductances add:
$$G_\text{par} = G_1 + G_2 + \dots, \qquad R_\text{par} = \frac{1}{\frac1{R_1} + \frac1{R_2} + \dots}.$$
For two resistors this is the "product over sum" rule, $R_1 \parallel R_2 = \dfrac{R_1 R_2}{R_1 + R_2}$.

A parallel combination is always **smaller** than its smallest resistor. A series combination is
always **larger** than its largest.

> **Intuition:** resistors in parallel are like extra lanes on a highway. Every added lane, even a slow one,
> lets *more* traffic through, so the total resistance can only drop. In series, every resistor is another
> toll booth the same cars must pass, so the resistances add.

steps.title: Recognizing series and parallel
steps.md:
The definitions are about **nodes**, not about how the drawing looks.

* **Series:** two elements share a node, and *nothing else* connects to that node. Then all of the
  current from one must go into the other.
* **Parallel:** both ends of the two elements connect to the *same pair of nodes*. Then they must share
  one voltage.

Two resistors drawn side by side aren't necessarily in parallel, and two drawn end to end aren't
necessarily in series. Always trace the nodes.

**Useful limiting cases:**

| combination | result | why |
|---|---|---|
| $R \parallel 0$ (a wire) | $0$ | the short carries everything |
| $R \parallel \infty$ (an open) | $R$ | the open carries nothing |
| $R + 0$ | $R$ | a wire adds no resistance |
| $R_\text{small} \parallel R_\text{big}$ | $\approx R_\text{small}$ | the smaller one dominates |
| $N$ equal $R$ in parallel | $R/N$ | conductances add |

Some networks can't be reduced at all. A **bridge** like the one in the node-analysis unit has no pair
of resistors that are in series or in parallel. For those, use node analysis.

q.name: A4b
q.prompt: A 1 kΩ resistor is in parallel with a 1 MΩ resistor. Roughly what is the combination?
q.why: $\frac{10^3 \cdot 10^6}{10^3 + 10^6} \approx 999$ Ω. A much larger resistor in parallel barely changes anything, because it carries only about 0.1% of the current.

options: No: some current can leave node $x$ through the third resistor
Yes: they're drawn end to end
Only if all three are equal
q.soln: No: some current can leave node $x$ through the third resistor
q.name: A4c
q.prompt: Resistors $R_a$ and $R_b$ connect end to end at node $x$, and a third resistor also connects to node $x$. Are $R_a$ and $R_b$ in series?
q.why: Series requires the *same* current. With another path at the shared node, KCL lets the currents differ.

q.name: A4
q.prompt: What is $6\,\Omega \parallel 3\,\Omega$?

q.name: A5
q.prompt: Three 12 Ω resistors are connected in parallel. What is the equivalent resistance?
q.why: $G = 3 \cdot \frac1{12} = \frac14$ S, so $R = 4$ Ω. $N$ equal resistors in parallel give $R/N$.

steps.title: Simplify first, then solve
steps.md: The 5 Ω and 3 Ω carry the same current, so they act like a single 8 Ω resistor from $e_1$ to ground. That eliminates node $e_2$, and one KCL equation at $e_1$ is enough: $$\frac{e_1 - 12}{4} - 2 + \frac{e_1}{8} = 0$$ Once you know $e_1$, return to the original circuit to find $e_2$. > **Watch out:** combining elements *hides* the nodes inside the combination. Here $e_2$ disappears > once you merge 5 Ω + 3 Ω. Never combine elements whose internal voltage or current you've been asked > for, or plan to come back and "un-combine" them (here with a voltage divider) afterward.

q.name: A6
q.prompt: Solve for $e_1$.

q.name: A7
q.prompt: Now find $e_2$, the node between the 5 Ω and 3 Ω resistors.
q.why: The series current is $e_1/8 = 5/3$ A, so $e_2 = 3\,\Omega \cdot \frac53 = 5$ V.

q.name: Q1
q.prompt: Quiz: a 4 Ω resistor is in series with the parallel combination of 6 Ω and 3 Ω. What is the total resistance?

q.name: Q2
q.prompt: Quiz: in the supernode circuit, change $V_B$ to 5 V (everything else the same). What is $e_1$?
q.why: Supernode KCL still gives $3e_1 + e_2 = 20$, and now $e_2 = e_1 - 5$. So $4e_1 = 25$ and $e_1 = 6.25$ V.

options: Conservation of charge holds for any closed surface
Voltage sources always carry zero current
KVL around the loop containing the source
q.soln: Conservation of charge holds for any closed surface
q.name: Q3
q.prompt: Quiz: what physical principle lets us write KCL around a supernode?
q.why: Charge can't pile up inside a closed surface in the lumped model, so the net current out of the surface is zero.

unit.title: Voltage and current dividers
unit.intro:
Two shortcuts you'll use constantly: series resistors split a voltage in proportion to
resistance, and parallel resistors split a current in proportion to conductance.

steps.title: Voltage dividers
steps.md:
Put $N$ resistors in series across a total voltage $v_T$. They all carry the same current
$i = v_T / (R_1 + \dots + R_N)$, so the voltage across the $j$-th one is

$$v_j = i\,R_j = \frac{R_j}{R_1 + R_2 + \dots + R_N}\, v_T.$$

Each resistor takes **its fraction of the total resistance**. For two resistors,
$v_2 = \dfrac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}\,v_T$.

A common use is scaling a large voltage down to something a measurement circuit can handle.

q.name: A1
q.prompt: A 10 V source is across a 1 kΩ resistor in series with a 4 kΩ resistor. What is the voltage across the 4 kΩ resistor?

q.name: A2
q.prompt: You want to monitor a 1000 V supply with a circuit that accepts at most 5 V. You build a divider with $R_1 + R_2 = 1$ MΩ and measure across $R_2$. What value should $R_2$ have?
q.why: You need $\frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2} = \frac{5}{1000} = 0.005$, so $R_2 = 0.005 \times 1\text{ M}\Omega = 5$ kΩ.

q.name: A3
q.prompt: How much power does that divider draw from the 1000 V supply?
q.why: $P = v^2 / R = 1000^2 / 10^6 = 1$ W, almost all of it in $R_1$. A larger total resistance would waste less power.

steps.title: Loading: the divider's hidden assumption
steps.md:
The divider formula assumes **nothing else draws current** from the middle node, so $R_1$ and $R_2$
carry the same current. Connect a load $R_L$ across $R_2$ and that assumption breaks. The load is in
parallel with $R_2$, so the bottom of the divider becomes $R_2 \parallel R_L$, which is smaller, and the
output drops:

$$v_\text{out} = \frac{R_2 \parallel R_L}{R_1 + R_2 \parallel R_L}\,v_T$$

**Rule of thumb:** the load barely matters when $R_L \gg R_2$ (10× or more). That's why voltmeters are
built with very large internal resistance (often 10 MΩ), so that measuring a voltage doesn't change it.

> **Intuition:** a divider is a weak voltage source. Its "stiffness" is limited by its resistors, and
> drawing current from it pulls its voltage down. The Thévenin unit makes this precise: a divider looks
> like a source of $\frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}v_T$ in series with $R_1 \parallel R_2$.

> **Watch out:** a divider is a good way to *measure* or *reference* a voltage, but a poor way to *power*
> something. The output sags with load, and the divider wastes power continuously.

q.name: A3b
q.prompt: A 10 V source feeds a divider of two 10 kΩ resistors. Unloaded, the output is 5 V. What is the output after a 10 kΩ load is connected across the bottom resistor?
q.why: The bottom becomes $10\text{k} \parallel 10\text{k} = 5$ kΩ, so $v = \frac{5}{10 + 5} \cdot 10 = 3.33$ V. A load equal to $R_2$ causes a large error.

steps.title: Current dividers
steps.md:
Put resistors in parallel carrying a total current $i_T$. They share a voltage
$v = i_T / (G_1 + \dots + G_N)$, so the current in the $j$-th one is

$$i_j = G_j\,v = \frac{G_j}{G_1 + G_2 + \dots + G_N}\, i_T.$$

Each branch takes **its fraction of the total conductance**. The *smaller* resistor carries the
*larger* current. For two resistors the formula flips compared with the voltage divider:

$$i_1 = \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}\, i_T, \qquad i_2 = \frac{R_1}{R_1 + R_2}\, i_T.$$

steps.title: Getting the divider formulas right
steps.md:
The two formulas look alike, which makes them easy to swap by accident. Two ways to keep them straight:

* **Check an extreme.** If $R_2 \to 0$, a voltage divider should give $v_2 \to 0$ (a short has no voltage),
  and $\frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}$ does. In a current divider, the branch with $R_1 \to 0$ should take *all* the
  current, and $i_1 = \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}\,i_T \to i_T$ does.
* **Think in the natural quantity.** A voltage divides by *resistance* (series elements share current,
  so $v \propto R$). A current divides by *conductance* (parallel elements share voltage, so $i \propto G$).
  Written with conductances, the current divider looks just like the voltage divider:
  $i_j = \frac{G_j}{\sum G}\,i_T$.

For three or more parallel branches, use the conductance form. The "other resistor on top" shortcut
only works for exactly two branches.

> **Intuition:** current prefers the easy path, but it doesn't *only* take the easy path. Each branch
> carries current in proportion to how easy it is ($G$). A 1 Ω branch next to a 2 Ω branch takes twice
> as much current, not all of it.

q.name: A4
q.prompt: A 6 A current splits between a 2 Ω and a 4 Ω resistor in parallel. How much flows through the 2 Ω resistor?
q.why: $i_{2\Omega} = \frac{4}{2 + 4} \cdot 6 = 4$ A. Note the *other* resistor's value goes on top.

steps.title: Example: a battery and two lamps
steps.md: Model the battery as an ideal 9 V source in series with an **internal resistance** of 0.5 Ω, and each lamp as a 2 Ω resistor. Combine and divide: * The lamps in parallel: $R_\text{eq} = 2 \parallel 2 = 1\ \Omega$. * Voltage divider for the lamp voltage: $v_L = \dfrac{R_\text{eq}}{R_\text{eq} + R_B}\,V_B$. * Series total for the battery current: $i_B = V_B / (R_B + R_\text{eq})$. * Current divider to split $i_B$ between the lamps.

q.name: A5
q.prompt: What is the lamp voltage $v_L$?
q.why: $v_L = \frac{1}{1 + 0.5} \cdot 9 = 6$ V. The internal resistance drops the other 3 V.

q.name: A6
q.prompt: What is the battery current $i_B$?

q.name: A7
q.prompt: How much current flows through each lamp?
q.why: Equal resistors split the current equally: $\frac{2}{2+2} \cdot 6 = 3$ A each.

steps.title: What the example teaches about real batteries
steps.md:
The internal resistance explains everyday behavior:

* The lamps get 6 V, not 9 V. The other 3 V is lost *inside* the battery, which turns
  $i_B^2 R_B = 6^2 \cdot 0.5 = 18$ W into heat. That's why batteries get warm under heavy load.
* The more lamps you add, the smaller $R_\text{eq}$ gets, the more current flows, and the more voltage
  is lost inside. Lights dim when you turn on more of them, and a car's headlights dim while it's starting.
* Shorting the terminals ($R_\text{eq} = 0$) gives the maximum current, $V_B / R_B = 18$ A here, with all
  the power dissipated inside the battery. This is why shorting a battery is dangerous.

> **Intuition:** the internal resistance is what makes a battery "weaker" under load. A healthy battery
> has a small $R_B$, so its voltage barely sags. An old one has a larger $R_B$: it may read 9 V on a
> voltmeter (almost no current) yet sag badly when you actually use it.

q.name: Q1
q.prompt: Quiz: 1 kΩ, 2 kΩ and 3 kΩ resistors are in series across 12 V. What is the voltage across the 3 kΩ resistor?

q.name: Q2
q.prompt: Quiz: 9 mA splits between 1 kΩ and 2 kΩ in parallel. How much flows through the 2 kΩ resistor?
q.why: $\frac{1}{1 + 2} \cdot 9 = 3$ mA. The larger resistor gets the smaller share.

q.name: Q3
q.prompt: Quiz: in the battery example, a third 2 Ω lamp is added in parallel. What is the new lamp voltage?
q.why: $R_\text{eq} = 2/3$ Ω, so $v_L = \frac{2/3}{2/3 + 1/2} \cdot 9 = \frac{36}{7} \approx 5.14$ V. More load means more current and a larger drop inside the battery.

unit.title: Linearity and superposition
unit.intro:
In a circuit built from linear elements and independent sources, every voltage and current
is a weighted sum of the sources. So you can find the response to each source on its own and add.

steps.title: Every answer is a linear combination of the sources
steps.md: KCL at $e$: $\;G_1(e - V) + G_2\,e - I = 0$, so $$e = \underbrace{\frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}}_{\text{weight on } V} V \;+\; \underbrace{\frac{R_1 R_2}{R_1 + R_2}}_{\text{weight on } I} I.$$ The node potential is a **linear combination** of the two sources, with weights set only by the resistors. This isn't a coincidence. Node analysis always gives $\mathbf{G}\,\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{s}$, where $\mathbf{s}$ is a linear sum of the source values. So $\mathbf{e} = \mathbf{G}^{-1}\mathbf{s}$ is linear in the sources too.

steps.title: Homogeneity and superposition
steps.md:
A linear system has two properties:

* **Homogeneity:** scale every input by $\alpha$ and every output scales by $\alpha$.
* **Superposition:** the response to a sum of inputs is the sum of the individual responses.

In circuits the *inputs* are the **independent sources**. To find one source's contribution,
set all the other independent sources to zero ("kill" them):

| source | set to zero | becomes |
|---|---|---|
| voltage source | $v = 0$ for any current | **short circuit** (a wire) |
| current source | $i = 0$ for any voltage | **open circuit** (removed) |

Solve each simpler circuit, then add the results.

> **Intuition:** "killing" a source means setting its *value* to zero while keeping what the element still
> enforces. A 0 V source still forces zero voltage across itself, which is exactly what a wire does. A
> 0 A source still forces zero current, which is exactly what a gap does.

> **Watch out:** when a voltage source is in series with a resistor and you kill the source, the
> **resistor stays**. Only the source turns into a wire. Similarly, a resistor in parallel with a killed
> current source stays connected.

steps.title: What makes a circuit linear?
steps.md:
Superposition needs every element to be **linear**: resistors ($v = Ri$), and (later) capacitors,
inductors and *linear* dependent sources. Each of these has an element law where doubling $i$ doubles $v$.

* A **diode** ($i \approx I_s e^{v/V_T}$) is not linear. A circuit containing one does not obey superposition.
* The **independent sources** are the *inputs*, not part of the linear system. That's why they are the
  things you turn on one at a time.

**Linearity lets you treat a circuit as a black box.** Any output is
$y = a_1 x_1 + a_2 x_2 + \dots$, with one weight per source. If you can measure the output for a few
source settings, you can solve for the weights and predict every other setting without ever looking
inside. Engineers use this constantly to characterize sensors and amplifiers.

q.name: A1b
q.prompt: An output reads 5 V when $V = 10$ V and $I = 0$, and 8 V when $V = 10$ V and $I = 2$ A. What would it read with $V = 0$ and $I = 1$ A?
q.why: Adding 2 A raised the output by $8 - 5 = 3$ V, so the weight on $I$ is 1.5 V per amp. With $V = 0$ and $I = 1$ A, the output is 1.5 V.

q.name: A1
q.prompt: When you set an independent current source to zero for superposition, what do you replace it with?
q.why: Zero current at any voltage is exactly what an open circuit does. A killed voltage source becomes a short (zero voltage at any current).

q.name: A2
q.prompt: In the circuit above, take $V = 10$ V, $R_1 = 2$ Ω, $R_2 = 3$ Ω, $I = 5$ A. With the current source killed (open), what is $e$?
q.why: Only a voltage divider is left: $e = \frac{3}{2 + 3} \cdot 10 = 6$ V.

q.name: A3
q.prompt: Now kill the voltage source (short) and keep $I = 5$ A. What is $e$?
q.why: The source sees $R_1 \parallel R_2 = 1.2$ Ω, so $e = 1.2 \cdot 5 = 6$ V.

q.name: A4
q.prompt: What is $e$ with both sources on?
q.why: By superposition, $6 + 6 = 12$ V. You can confirm with one KCL equation: $(e-10)/2 + e/3 = 5$ gives $e = 12$ V.

steps.title: Superposition can be faster than solving equations
steps.md: Node analysis would give three simultaneous equations here. Superposition breaks it into two circuits you can solve by inspection. * **$I_A$ alone** ($I_B$ open): no current can flow in $R_2$, so $I_A$ flows through $R_1$ and $R_3$ in series. $e_3 = I_A R_3$ and $e_1 = I_A(R_1 + R_3)$. * **$I_B$ alone** ($I_A$ open): $I_B$ flows through $R_2$ and $R_3$, and $R_1$ carries nothing. $e_3 = I_B R_3$ and $e_1 = e_3 = I_B R_3$. Add the two cases to get each node potential. As a bonus, you can see how much each source contributes. > **Intuition:** this circuit is a real thermal model. Think of $I_A$ and $I_B$ as heat from two chips > on one heat sink, the resistors as thermal resistances, and the node potentials as temperature rises. > Superposition says each chip's heat raises every temperature independently. The shared resistor $R_3$ > (the heat sink to air) is where both chips' heat ends up, which is why $e_3$ depends on $I_A + I_B$.

q.name: A5
q.prompt: What is $e_3$ with both sources on?
q.why: $e_3 = I_A R_3 + I_B R_3 = (2 + 1) \cdot 3 = 9$ V. Both source currents end up flowing down through $R_3$.

q.name: A6
q.prompt: What is $e_1$ with both sources on?

steps.title: Why power does not superpose
steps.md:
In the first example, each source alone gave $e = 6$ V, so the 3 Ω resistor $R_2$ would absorb
$6^2/3 = 12$ W in each case. Adding those gives 24 W. But with both sources on, $e = 12$ V, and
$R_2$ actually absorbs $12^2/3 = 48$ W, twice as much.

The reason is that power is $v^2/R$. Squaring a sum isn't the sum of squares:
$(v_A + v_B)^2 = v_A^2 + v_B^2 + 2v_A v_B$. The cross term $2v_A v_B$ is the part you lose.

**The rule:** superpose voltages and currents, *then* compute power from the total.

> **When is superposition worth it?** It shines when there are a few sources and each single-source
> circuit simplifies to something you can do by inspection (a divider, a series path). It's also great when
> you want to know *how much each source contributes*. With many sources, or when the single-source
> circuits are still messy, one node analysis is usually faster.

q.name: Q1
q.prompt: Quiz: in the first circuit, an output is 3 V when $V = 1$ V acts alone and 2 V when $I = 1$ A acts alone. What is the output when $V = 4$ V and $I = 2$ A?
q.why: Linearity: $3 \cdot 4 + 2 \cdot 2 = 16$ V.

q.name: Q2
q.prompt: Quiz: in the two-source circuit, find $e_2$.
q.why: $I_A$ alone gives $e_2 = e_3 = I_A R_3 = 6$ V (no current in $R_2$). $I_B$ alone gives $I_B(R_2 + R_3) = 5$ V. The total is 11 V.

options: The power dissipated in a resistor
q.soln: The power dissipated in a resistor
q.name: Q3
q.prompt: Quiz: which of these can you not find by adding single-source results?
q.why: Power is $i^2 R$, which is quadratic, not linear, in the sources. Superpose the currents or voltages first, then compute the power.

unit.title: Equivalent circuits: the Thévenin model
unit.intro:
Any network of linear resistors and sources, seen from two terminals, behaves exactly
like one voltage source in series with one resistor.

steps.title: A port and its i–v line
steps.md:
Pick two terminals of a network (a **port**), with port voltage $v_x$ and current $i_x$ flowing
*into* the + terminal. Imagine driving the port with a test current source $i_x$. By superposition,
$v_x$ is the sum of

* the response to the network's own sources with $i_x = 0$ (the port left open), and
* the response to $i_x$ alone with the internal sources killed, which is just $i_x$ times a resistance.

$$v_x = V_\text{Th} + R_\text{Th}\, i_x$$

So the port's $i$–$v$ characteristic is always a **straight line**. That's not obvious: the network
might contain hundreds of parts. Linearity guarantees that all that complexity collapses to a line, and
two numbers describe it:

* $V_\text{Th}$, the **open-circuit voltage** (the $v_x$ intercept, where $i_x = 0$), and
* $R_\text{Th}$, the resistance seen looking into the port with all independent sources killed
  (the inverse slope).

steps.title: The Thévenin equivalent
steps.md: A source $V_\text{Th}$ in series with $R_\text{Th}$ has exactly that line, $v_x = V_\text{Th} + R_\text{Th}\,i_x$. So **as far as anything connected to the port can tell**, the two are identical. This lets you replace a big, messy linear network with two components and focus on the part you care about. > **Intuition:** $V_\text{Th}$ says how hard the network "pushes" when nothing is connected. > $R_\text{Th}$ says how much that push sags as you draw current. A stiff source (a good bench > supply) has small $R_\text{Th}$. A weak one (a sensor, a divider) has large $R_\text{Th}$.

steps.title: Example
steps.md: **$V_\text{Th}$:** with nothing attached, find $v_x$. One node equation, or superposition: $$V_\text{Th} = \frac{3}{6 + 3}\cdot 12 + (6 \parallel 3)\cdot 1.$$ **$R_\text{Th}$:** short the 12 V source, open the 1 A source, and look into the port. You see 6 Ω in parallel with 3 Ω.

q.name: A1
q.prompt: What is $V_\text{Th}$?

q.name: A2
q.prompt: What is $R_\text{Th}$?
q.why: With the sources killed, $6 \parallel 3 = 2$ Ω.

steps.title: Checking with the short-circuit current
steps.md:
Short the port ($v_x = 0$) and measure the current that comes out, $i_\text{sc} = -i_x$. On the
Thévenin line, $v_x = 0$ happens at $i_x = -V_\text{Th}/R_\text{Th}$, so

$$R_\text{Th} = \frac{V_\text{oc}}{i_\text{sc}}.$$

That gives a second way to find $R_\text{Th}$, or a check on the first. (On a real power source,
shorting the terminals can be dangerous. It's fine on paper.)

q.name: A3
q.prompt: Short the port in the example. What current $i_\text{sc}$ flows out through the short?
q.why: With the port shorted, the top node is at 0 V. The 3 Ω carries nothing, the 12 V source drives $12/6 = 2$ A through the short, and the 1 A source adds 1 A, for $i_\text{sc} = 3$ A. Check: $V_\text{oc}/i_\text{sc} = 6/3 = 2$ Ω. ✓

q.name: A4
q.prompt: Connect a 4 Ω load to the port. What is the voltage across it?
q.why: Use the Thévenin model: a voltage divider of 2 Ω and 4 Ω, so $\frac{4}{2 + 4} \cdot 6 = 4$ V. No need to re-solve the whole network.

steps.title: Three ways to find R_Th
steps.md:
| method | how | when it works |
|---|---|---|
| **Kill and combine** | Kill the independent sources, then reduce with series/parallel | Only independent sources and resistors, and the network reduces |
| **Open/short** | $R_\text{Th} = V_\text{oc} / i_\text{sc}$ | Whenever $V_\text{oc}$ and $i_\text{sc}$ aren't both zero |
| **Test source** | Kill independent sources, apply $i_\text{test}$, find $v_\text{test}$; $R_\text{Th} = v_\text{test}/i_\text{test}$ | Always, including dependent sources (next units) |

It's good practice to find $R_\text{Th}$ two different ways. If they disagree, one of them has a mistake.

> **Watch out:** "equivalent" means equivalent **at the port only**. The Thévenin model reproduces every
> voltage and current *outside* the box, but not what happens *inside*. With the port open, the example
> network still dissipates power internally: the 6 Ω and 3 Ω absorb 6 W and 12 W, while the Thévenin
> model, carrying no current, dissipates nothing. Don't use the model to compute the network's own power.

options: Short the voltage sources and open the current sources
Open the voltage sources and short the current sources
q.soln: Short the voltage sources and open the current sources
q.name: A5
q.prompt: To find $R_\text{Th}$, what do you do with the network's independent sources?
q.why: $R_\text{Th}$ is the response to the external current alone, so the internal sources are set to zero.

steps.title: Going further: maximum power transfer
steps.md:
Which load $R_L$ draws the most power from a Thévenin source? The load current is
$V_\text{Th}/(R_\text{Th} + R_L)$, so

$$P_L = \frac{V_\text{Th}^2\,R_L}{(R_\text{Th} + R_L)^2}.$$

It's zero for $R_L = 0$ (no voltage) and for $R_L \to \infty$ (no current), so it peaks somewhere in between.
Setting $dP_L/dR_L = 0$ gives

$$R_L = R_\text{Th}, \qquad P_\text{max} = \frac{V_\text{Th}^2}{4R_\text{Th}}.$$

This is **impedance matching**, used for antennas, audio amplifiers and speakers. But at the matched
load, the same power is burned in $R_\text{Th}$ as in the load, so efficiency is only 50%. Power
utilities do the opposite: they keep $R_L \gg R_\text{Th}$ for high efficiency.

q.name: A6
q.prompt: For the example network ($V_\text{Th} = 6$ V, $R_\text{Th} = 2$ Ω), what is the most power any load resistor can draw?
q.why: $P_\text{max} = V_\text{Th}^2 / (4 R_\text{Th}) = 36/8 = 4.5$ W, at $R_L = 2$ Ω. Check: 1.5 A through 2 Ω gives $1.5^2 \cdot 2 = 4.5$ W.

q.name: Q1
q.prompt: Quiz: a network has an open-circuit voltage of 5 V and a short-circuit current of 0.5 A. What is $R_\text{Th}$?
q.why: $R_\text{Th} = V_\text{oc}/i_\text{sc} = 5/0.5 = 10$ Ω.

q.name: Q2
q.prompt: Quiz: a battery reads 9 V with nothing connected, and 8 V while it delivers 1 A to a load. Model it as a Thévenin equivalent. What is its internal resistance?
q.why: Delivering 1 A drops $9 - 8 = 1$ V across $R_\text{Th}$, so $R_\text{Th} = 1$ Ω.

q.name: Q3
q.prompt: Quiz: for the example network ($V_\text{Th} = 6$ V, $R_\text{Th} = 2$ Ω), you push $i_x = 1$ A into the + terminal. What is $v_x$?
q.why: $v_x = V_\text{Th} + R_\text{Th}\,i_x = 6 + 2 \cdot 1 = 8$ V.

unit.title: Thévenin and Norton equivalents
unit.intro:
The same straight i–v line can be produced by a current source in parallel with a resistor.
Learn to find either model and to switch between them.

steps.title: Finding a Thévenin model
steps.md: Two numbers describe the port: the open-circuit voltage and the resistance with sources killed. * **$V_\text{Th} = V_\text{oc}$:** with the port open, $R_1$ carries no current, so the whole $I_1$ goes through $R_3$ and down through $R_2$. * **$R_\text{Th}$:** open $I_1$. Then $R_3$ dangles (one end goes nowhere), and you see $R_1$ in series with $R_2$.

q.name: A1
q.prompt: What is $V_\text{Th}$?
q.why: $V_\text{Th} = I_1 R_2 = 2 \cdot 6 = 12$ V, because no current flows in $R_1$ with the port open.

q.name: A2
q.prompt: What is $R_\text{Th}$?
q.why: With $I_1$ opened, $R_3$ carries nothing, so $R_\text{Th} = R_1 + R_2 = 9$ Ω.

options: It is in series with an ideal current source, which sets the current no matter what $R_3$ is
q.soln: It is in series with an ideal current source, which sets the current no matter what $R_3$ is
q.name: A3
q.prompt: Why doesn't the 5 Ω resistor $R_3$ appear in either answer?
q.why: $R_3$ changes the voltage across the current source, but not the current it delivers, so nothing the port sees depends on $R_3$.

steps.title: The Norton equivalent
steps.md: A current source $I_N$ in parallel with $R_N$ gives $v_x = (I_N + i_x)\,R_N = I_N R_N + R_N\,i_x$. That is the same straight line, so it can match any linear port too: * $R_N = R_\text{Th}$ (the same resistance looking in with sources killed), * $I_N = i_\text{sc}$, the current out of the port when it's shorted, * and the two models are linked by $V_\text{Th} = I_N R_N$. Which model you use is a matter of convenience. Converting back and forth (**source transformation**) is often a fast way to simplify a circuit. **Reading the models off the $i$–$v$ line.** Plot the port's line with $v_x$ on the horizontal axis. Where it crosses $i_x = 0$ is $V_\text{oc} = V_\text{Th}$. Where it crosses $v_x = 0$ is $-I_N$. Its slope is $1/R_\text{Th}$. Any two of these three numbers give the third, which is why you only need two measurements to model a linear port. > **Intuition:** Norton models suit devices that behave like current sources: a solar cell, a photodiode, > or a transistor's output all deliver a roughly fixed current, with a large parallel resistance that leaks a little of it.

q.name: A4
q.prompt: Find the Norton current $I_N$ for the example network.
q.why: $I_N = V_\text{Th}/R_\text{Th} = 12/9 = 4/3$ A. Directly: with the port shorted, $I_1$ splits between $R_2$ and $R_1$, and $R_1$ gets $\frac{6}{3 + 6} \cdot 2 = \frac43$ A.

q.name: A5
q.prompt: Convert a Norton model of 2 A in parallel with 5 Ω into a Thévenin model. What is $V_\text{Th}$?
q.why: $V_\text{Th} = I_N R_N = 2 \cdot 5 = 10$ V, with $R_\text{Th} = 5$ Ω.

steps.title: Source transformations as a simplification tool
steps.md:
Because the two models are interchangeable, you can swap one for the other *in the middle of a circuit*
to make things combine. A voltage source $V$ in series with $R$ can become a current source $V/R$ in
parallel with $R$, and back.

**Example.** A 12 V source in series with 3 Ω drives a node that also has 6 Ω to ground. What does
that node look like?

1. Transform: 12 V in series with 3 Ω becomes $12/3 = 4$ A in parallel with 3 Ω.
2. Now 3 Ω and 6 Ω are in parallel: $3 \parallel 6 = 2$ Ω.
3. Transform back: 4 A in parallel with 2 Ω becomes $4 \cdot 2 = 8$ V in series with 2 Ω.

So the whole thing is a Thévenin source of 8 V with 2 Ω, matching the divider result
$\frac{6}{3+6}\cdot 12 = 8$ V.

> **Intuition:** use Thévenin form when things connect in **series** with the source (voltages add along a
> chain). Use Norton form when things connect in **parallel** (currents add at a node). Switching forms
> lets each step become a simple combination.

> **Watch out:** an **ideal** voltage source ($R = 0$) has no Norton form, since $I_N = V/0$ is infinite. An
> ideal current source ($R = \infty$) has no Thévenin form. Transformations need the resistor.

q.name: A6
q.prompt: Transform 5 mA in parallel with 2 kΩ into a Thévenin form, then add a 3 kΩ resistor in series. What is the short-circuit current of the result?
q.why: The Thévenin form is $5\text{ mA} \cdot 2\text{ k}\Omega = 10$ V with 2 kΩ. Adding 3 kΩ gives 10 V with 5 kΩ, so $i_\text{sc} = 10/5\text{k} = 2$ mA.

options: No: it would need an infinite current source
Yes: 5 A in parallel with 1 Ω
Yes: 0 A in parallel with an open circuit
q.soln: No: it would need an infinite current source
q.name: A7
q.prompt: Does an ideal 5 V voltage source, with no series resistance, have a Norton equivalent?
q.why: $R_\text{Th} = 0$, so $I_N = V_\text{Th}/R_\text{Th}$ is undefined. Its $i$–$v$ line is vertical, and no parallel model can produce that.

q.name: Q1
q.prompt: Quiz: a Norton model has $I_N = 3$ mA and $R_N = 2$ kΩ. What is its open-circuit voltage?
q.why: $V_\text{oc} = I_N R_N = 3\text{ mA} \cdot 2\text{ k}\Omega = 6$ V.

q.name: Q2
q.prompt: Quiz: connect a 3 Ω load across the example network's port. What current flows through the load?
q.why: Using the Thévenin model: $12 / (9 + 3) = 1$ A.

q.name: Q3
q.prompt: Quiz: a port has $V_\text{oc} = 10$ V and $i_\text{sc} = 2$ A. What is $R_N$?
q.why: $R_N = R_\text{Th} = V_\text{oc}/i_\text{sc} = 5$ Ω.

unit.title: Dependent sources
unit.intro:
Sources whose value is set by a voltage or current somewhere else in the circuit. They model
amplifiers and transistors, and they change how you find equivalent resistances.

steps.title: Four kinds of dependent source
steps.md:
An **independent** source is an input to the circuit: its value doesn't depend on anything else.
A **dependent** (controlled) source imposes a voltage or current that is a function of a voltage
or current *measured elsewhere* in the circuit. It is drawn as a diamond.

| name | it outputs | controlled by |
|---|---|---|
| VCVS | voltage | a voltage |
| VCCS | current | a voltage |
| CCVS | voltage | a current |
| CCCS | current | a current |

A **linear** dependent source has the form (output) $= k \times$ (control). Think of it as a two-port
device: one port measures without disturbing anything, and the other port acts.

The constant has units that match its type: a VCVS gain is unitless (V/V), a VCCS has a
**transconductance** $g_m$ in siemens (A/V), a CCVS has a **transresistance** $r_m$ in ohms (V/A),
and a CCCS gain is unitless (A/A).

> **Why bother with them?** Resistors only ever absorb power, so a network of resistors and
> independent sources can never *amplify* a signal. Real amplifiers (transistors, op-amps) draw energy
> from a power supply and use a small input to control a large output. A dependent source is the simplest
> linear model of that: it can deliver power, and the power supply it implies is simply not drawn.

q.name: A1
q.prompt: A transistor model has a current source whose value is $g_m v_\pi$, where $v_\pi$ is a voltage elsewhere. What type of dependent source is it?
q.why: It outputs a **current** controlled by a **voltage**: a voltage-controlled current source. $g_m$ has units of siemens.

steps.title: Dependent sources in node analysis
steps.md: Treat the dependent source like an ordinary source in KCL. Then write its control variable in terms of node potentials: here $i_1 = (V_A - e)/R_1$. KCL at $e$ (currents in = currents out): $$\frac{V_A - e}{R_1} + k\,\frac{V_A - e}{R_1} = \frac{e}{R_2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad e = \frac{(k+1)R_2}{R_1 + (k+1)R_2}\,V_A$$ The dependent source makes $R_2$ look $(k+1)$ times larger to the rest of the circuit. **The general recipe** for node analysis with dependent sources: 1. Write KCL as usual, treating each dependent source as if it were independent (call its value $4i_1$, say). 2. Write each **control variable** in terms of node potentials: $i_1 = (V_A - e)/R_1$. 3. Substitute, collect terms and solve. > **Watch out:** after step 3, the conductance matrix is usually **no longer symmetric**, and its > diagonal may not dominate. That's expected with dependent sources, not a sign of a mistake. If a > dependent *voltage* source floats between two nodes, use a supernode just as with an independent one. > **Intuition:** why does $R_2$ look bigger? For every 1 A that comes through $R_1$, the dependent source > adds 4 A more into the same node. $R_2$ must carry all 5 A, so its voltage is 5 times what that 1 A alone > would produce. To the source $V_A$, it's as if $R_2$ were 5 times larger.

q.name: A2
q.prompt: With $V_A = 10$ V, $R_1 = 5$ Ω, $R_2 = 1$ Ω and $k = 4$, what is $e$?
q.why: $e = \frac{5 \cdot 1}{5 + 5 \cdot 1} \cdot 10 = 5$ V.

q.name: A3
q.prompt: What current does the dependent source supply?
q.why: $i_1 = (10 - 5)/5 = 1$ A, so the source supplies $4 i_1 = 4$ A. Check KCL: $1 + 4 = 5$ A $= e/R_2$. ✓

steps.title: Never kill a dependent source
steps.md:
For superposition, Thévenin and Norton, you kill only the **independent** sources. Dependent
sources are components that describe how the circuit behaves, not inputs, so they stay.

Because they stay, series/parallel shortcuts usually don't work. Use the **test-source method**
instead:

1. Kill the independent sources.
2. Apply a test current $i_\text{test}$ to the port (or a test voltage).
3. Solve for the response $v_\text{test}$.
4. $R_\text{Th} = v_\text{test} / i_\text{test}$.

Since the circuit is linear, the value of $i_\text{test}$ doesn't matter. Pick 1 A to make the arithmetic
easy, then $R_\text{Th}$ is just the number you get for $v_\text{test}$.

**Surprises dependent sources can produce:**

* A network with **no independent sources** has $V_\text{Th} = 0$, but it can still have a nonzero
  $R_\text{Th}$. It looks like a plain resistor.
* $R_\text{Th}$ can be **negative**. Then the port *delivers* power when you push current into it. That's
  impossible with resistors alone, but fine with a dependent source drawing on a hidden supply.

q.name: A4b
q.prompt: A 100 Ω resistor is in series with a CCVS whose voltage is $r\,i$, where $i$ is the current through the resistor and the polarity adds to the resistor's voltage. With $r = -150$ Ω, what resistance does the pair present?
q.why: $v = 100\,i + r\,i = (100 - 150)\,i = -50\,i$. A negative resistance: push current in and the pair delivers power.

q.name: A4
q.prompt: Remove $V_A$ from the example and look into the left terminals, where $V_A$ was. Push $i_\text{test}$ in through $R_1$, so $i_1 = i_\text{test}$. What resistance do you see?
q.why: $R_2$ carries $(k+1)\,i_\text{test}$, so $e = (k+1) R_2\, i_\text{test}$ and $v_\text{test} = e + R_1 i_\text{test}$. So $R = (k+1)R_2 + R_1 = 5 + 5 = 10$ Ω.

steps.title: Example: an amplifier model
steps.md: This is the standard small-signal model of a transistor amplifier. The input sets $v_\pi = v_i$. The output port has $g_m v_\pi$ flowing down through $r_o$, so $$v_o = -g_m r_o\, v_i.$$ If $g_m r_o > 1$, you get **voltage gain**. The minus sign is real: a common-emitter amplifier inverts its input, because the current $g_m v_\pi$ is pulled *down* through $r_o$. The output's Thévenin resistance: kill $v_i$, which makes $v_\pi = 0$ and turns off the dependent source, leaving $r_o$. The input side affects the output, but not the other way around. Dependent sources are *non-reciprocal*.

q.name: A5
q.prompt: With $g_m = 40$ mS and $r_o = 10$ kΩ, what is the voltage gain $v_o / v_i$?

q.name: A6
q.prompt: What is the Thévenin (output) resistance seen at $v_o$?
q.why: With $v_i$ killed, $v_\pi = 0$, so the dependent source is off and only $r_o = 10$ kΩ remains.

q.name: Q1
q.prompt: Quiz: in the CCCS circuit, set $k = 0$ (the dependent source is off). What is $e$?
q.why: It's now a plain divider: $\frac{1}{5 + 1} \cdot 10 = \frac53$ V. The dependent source tripled $e$.

q.name: Q2
q.prompt: Quiz: in the amplifier model with $g_m = 2$ mS and $r_o = 50$ kΩ, what is $v_o$ for $v_i = 10$ mV?

options: 2, with the dependent source kept in both
q.soln: 2, with the dependent source kept in both
q.name: Q3
q.prompt: Quiz: you are using superposition on a circuit with two independent sources and one dependent source. How many single-source circuits do you solve?
q.why: Only independent sources are inputs. The dependent source is a component and stays in every case.

unit.title: Capacitors and first-order circuits
unit.intro:
Capacitors store energy and remember their past, so circuits with them are described by
differential equations. Solve the simplest one, an RC circuit charging up.

steps.title: The capacitor
steps.md:
Two conductors separated by an insulator store equal and opposite charge $\pm q$ when there's a voltage
between them. For a linear capacitor the charge is proportional to the voltage:

$$q = C\,v \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad i = \frac{dq}{dt} = C\,\frac{dv}{dt}$$

$C$ is in **farads** (coulombs per volt). A parallel-plate capacitor has $C = \varepsilon A / d$.
The current into one terminal equals the current out of the other. No net charge builds up, only
separated charge.

**Energy.** Integrating the power $v\,i = v\,C\,\frac{dv}{dt}$ gives the stored energy
$$W = \tfrac12\, C\, v^2.$$

steps.title: Building intuition for capacitors
steps.md:
> **Intuition:** think of a capacitor as a water tank. The **voltage** is the water level, the **current**
> is the flow rate in, and the **capacitance** is the tank's floor area. A wide tank (large $C$) needs a lot
> of water to raise its level a little. $i = C\,dv/dt$ is exactly "flow = area × rate of rise".

Two consequences you'll use constantly:

* **Constant voltage means zero current.** If $v$ isn't changing, $i = 0$. At DC, after everything
  settles, a capacitor acts like an **open circuit**.
* **A fast-changing voltage needs a large current.** The faster you try to change $v$, the more current
  you need. Over very short times a capacitor resists any change in voltage, acting like a battery holding
  its present value.

**Combining capacitors** works the *opposite* way from resistors:

* **Parallel:** charges add at the same voltage, so $C_\text{eq} = C_1 + C_2$.
* **Series:** the same charge sits on each, and the voltages add, so $\frac1{C_\text{eq}} = \frac1{C_1} + \frac1{C_2}$.

q.name: A0
q.prompt: What is the equivalent capacitance of 2 µF and 3 µF in series?
q.why: $\frac{2 \cdot 3}{2 + 3} = 1.2$ µF, smaller than either one. In parallel they would give 5 µF.

q.name: A1
q.prompt: How much energy does a 10 µF capacitor store at 5 V?

q.name: A2
q.prompt: The voltage across a 2 µF capacitor ramps up at 3 V per millisecond. What current flows into it?

steps.title: The state property
steps.md:
Integrate $i = C\,dv/dt$:
$$v(t_1) = v(t_0) + \frac1C \int_{t_0}^{t_1} i\,dt.$$

The capacitor's voltage depends on its whole history of current. It has **memory**, and $v$ is its
**state**. As long as the current is finite, the integral over a vanishingly short time is zero, so

$$v_C(0^+) = v_C(0^-).$$

**Capacitor voltage cannot jump.** This is what you use to find initial conditions after a switch moves.

q.name: A3
q.prompt: A switch flips at $t = 0$. The capacitor was at 3 V just before. What is its voltage just after, assuming no infinite currents?
q.why: Capacitor voltage is continuous: $v_C(0^+) = v_C(0^-) = 3$ V.

steps.title: Charging an RC circuit
steps.md: The capacitor starts uncharged and the switch closes at $t = 0$. For $t > 0$, KCL at the top of the capacitor gives $$\frac{v_C - V_I}{R} + C\frac{dv_C}{dt} = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad v_C + RC\,\frac{dv_C}{dt} = V_I.$$ That's a first-order linear differential equation. Solve it in three steps. 1. **Particular solution:** any function that works. A constant does: $v_{C,p} = V_I$. 2. **Homogeneous solution:** solve $v_C + RC\,\dot v_C = 0$. Try $Ae^{st}$: $1 + RCs = 0$, so $s = -1/RC$ and $v_{C,h} = A e^{-t/\tau}$ with the **time constant** $\tau = RC$. 3. **Total = particular + homogeneous**, $v_C = V_I + A e^{-t/\tau}$. Pick $A$ to match the initial condition $v_C(0^+) = 0$: $A = -V_I$. $$v_C(t) = V_I\left(1 - e^{-t/RC}\right), \quad t \ge 0$$

steps.title: Why the response is exponential
steps.md:
Rearrange the differential equation:

$$\frac{dv_C}{dt} = \frac{V_I - v_C}{RC}$$

The capacitor charges at a rate **proportional to how far it still has to go**. At first the gap is
the whole $V_I$, so the current $(V_I - v_C)/R$ is largest and the voltage rises fastest. As $v_C$
approaches $V_I$, the resistor's voltage shrinks, the current shrinks, and the charging slows down.
It never quite arrives. Any quantity whose rate of change is proportional to its distance from a
target behaves this way. That's the definition of an exponential approach.

**Units check:** $RC$ is in $\Omega \cdot \text{F} = \frac{\text{V}}{\text{A}} \cdot \frac{\text{A·s}}{\text{V}} = \text{s}$.
A larger $R$ means less current (a slower fill), and a larger $C$ means a bigger tank. Either one makes the circuit slower.

> **Watch out:** the capacitor's *voltage* is continuous, but its *current* is not. When the switch closes,
> $i_C$ jumps from 0 to $V_I/R$ instantly, then decays as $\frac{V_I}{R}e^{-t/RC}$.

q.name: A4
q.prompt: With $R = 1$ kΩ and $C = 1$ µF, what is the time constant?

q.name: A5
q.prompt: With $V_I = 5$ V and $\tau = 1$ ms, what is $v_C$ at $t = 2$ ms?

steps.title: Sketching exponentials
steps.md:
Every first-order natural response has the shape $e^{-t/\tau}$. A few values are worth memorizing:

| $t$ | $\tau$ | $2\tau$ | $3\tau$ | $5\tau$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $e^{-t/\tau}$ | 0.37 | 0.14 | 0.05 | 0.007 |

* Each time constant, what's left shrinks by a factor of $1/e \approx 0.37$.
* After $3\tau$ the response is 95% of the way there, and after $5\tau$ it's above 99%.
* The initial slope, if it continued as a straight line, would finish the whole change in exactly one $\tau$.

q.name: A6
q.prompt: An RC circuit charging toward 10 V from 0 V: what voltage does it reach after one time constant?
q.why: $10\,(1 - e^{-1}) \approx 10 \cdot 0.632 = 6.32$ V. Each $\tau$ removes 63% of the remaining gap.

steps.title: Where does the energy go?
steps.md:
Charge a capacitor from 0 to $V_I$ through a resistor. The source pushes total charge $Q = CV_I$ at a fixed
voltage $V_I$, so it supplies

$$W_\text{source} = Q\,V_I = C V_I^2.$$

But the capacitor ends up storing only $\tfrac12 C V_I^2$. The other half is turned into heat in the
resistor, $\int i^2 R\,dt = \tfrac12 C V_I^2$, **no matter what $R$ is**. A small $R$ means a big current for a
short time, and a large $R$ means a small current for a long time. The integral comes out the same.

> **Intuition:** this 50% loss is built into charging from a fixed voltage. Circuits that need to be
> efficient (adiabatic logic, some power converters) instead ramp the source up gradually, keeping the
> voltage across the resistor small the whole time.

q.name: A7
q.prompt: A 1 µF capacitor is charged from 0 to 10 V by a 10 V source through a resistor. How much energy is dissipated in the resistor?
q.why: The source supplies $CV^2 = 100\ \mu$J. The capacitor stores $\tfrac12 CV^2 = 50\ \mu$J, and the remaining 50 µJ heats the resistor, independent of $R$.

q.name: Q1
q.prompt: Quiz: what is the time constant of a 10 kΩ resistor with a 100 nF capacitor?

q.name: Q2
q.prompt: Quiz: with $\tau = 2$ ms, roughly how long until the capacitor is 95% charged?
q.why: $e^{-3} \approx 0.05$, so 95% takes about $3\tau = 6$ ms.

q.name: Q3
q.prompt: Quiz: how much energy goes into a 2 µF capacitor when it charges from 1 V to 3 V?

options: That would need an infinite current, since $i = C\,dv/dt$
Because the energy $\tfrac12 Cv^2$ must always be zero
q.soln: That would need an infinite current, since $i = C\,dv/dt$
q.name: Q4
q.prompt: Quiz: why can a capacitor's voltage not change instantly in a real circuit?
q.why: A jump in $v$ makes $dv/dt$ infinite. With finite currents (no ideal impulses), $v_C$ is continuous.

unit.title: First-order circuits by inspection
unit.intro:
Skip the differential equation. With constant inputs, any first-order response is set by
three numbers you can read off the circuit: where it starts, where it ends, and how fast it gets there.

steps.title: Capacitors and inductors side by side
steps.md:
| | capacitor | inductor |
|---|---|---|
| element law | $i = C\,\dfrac{dv}{dt}$ | $v = L\,\dfrac{di}{dt}$ |
| stored energy | $\tfrac12 C v^2$ | $\tfrac12 L i^2$ |
| state (continuous) | voltage $v_C$ | current $i_L$ |
| time constant | $\tau = R_\text{Th}\,C$ | $\tau = L / R_\text{Th}$ |

$R_\text{Th}$ is the Thévenin resistance the capacitor or inductor sees looking back into the rest of
the circuit, with independent sources killed. Every voltage and current in a first-order circuit
decays with the **same** $\tau$.

q.name: A1
q.prompt: An inductor of 10 mH sees a Thévenin resistance of 100 Ω. What is the time constant?

steps.title: The inductor's personality
steps.md:
The inductor is the **dual** of the capacitor: swap $v \leftrightarrow i$ and $C \leftrightarrow L$ and every
statement carries over.

> **Intuition:** an inductor is like a heavy flywheel, or water moving through a long pipe. The current
> has momentum. Voltage is the push needed to speed it up or slow it down ($v = L\,di/dt$), and the
> current can't stop instantly any more than a moving train can.

**Why $\tau = L/R$ but $\tau = RC$?** A larger $L$ means more "inertia", so it's slower. A larger $R$
takes energy out faster, so it's *quicker* for an inductor. For a capacitor, a larger $R$ chokes the
charging current, so it's *slower*. Both expressions come out in seconds.

**Inductive kick.** Suppose 1 A flows in an inductor and you open a switch so that the only path left
is a 1 kΩ resistor. The current must still be 1 A at $t = 0^+$, so the resistor's voltage jumps to
$1\text{ A} \times 1\text{ k}\Omega = 1000$ V. With no path at all, the voltage rises until something
arcs. That's the spark in a car's ignition coil, and why relay coils are protected with a "flyback" diode.

q.name: A1b
q.prompt: An inductor carries 1 A. A switch opens, leaving the inductor connected only to a 1 kΩ resistor. What is the resistor's voltage at $t = 0^+$?
q.why: Inductor current is continuous, so 1 A still flows at $0^+$, now forced through 1 kΩ: $v = 1000$ V. It then decays with $\tau = L/1\text{k}\Omega$.

steps.title: DC steady state
steps.md:
Long after the last change ($t \gg \tau$), with constant inputs, nothing is changing:

* $dv_C/dt = 0$, so $i_C = 0$. **A capacitor acts as an open circuit.**
* $di_L/dt = 0$, so $v_L = 0$. **An inductor acts as a short circuit.**

That gives the final value $x(\infty)$ from a purely resistive circuit. Right after a switch moves,
use continuity: $v_C(0^+) = v_C(0^-)$ and $i_L(0^+) = i_L(0^-)$.

q.name: A2
q.prompt: In DC steady state, an inductor behaves like:
q.why: Constant current means $v_L = L\,di/dt = 0$: zero voltage at any current, which is a wire.

steps.title: The three-number recipe
steps.md:
For any quantity $x(t)$ in a first-order circuit with constant inputs, for $t > 0$:

$$x(t) = x(\infty) + \big[x(0^+) - x(\infty)\big]\,e^{-t/\tau}$$

1. **Final value** $x(\infty)$: replace C by an open (L by a short) and solve.
2. **Initial value** $x(0^+)$: use the capacitor voltage (inductor current) from just before the switch,
   then solve the circuit at $t = 0^+$ with C as a voltage source (L as a current source).
3. **Time constant** $\tau$: find $R_\text{Th}$ seen by the C or L with sources killed.

**Details that trip people up:**

* For $x(0^+)$, first find the **state** at $0^-$ ($v_C$ or $i_L$, from the circuit *before* the switch,
  usually in DC steady state). Then draw the circuit *after* the switch, with the capacitor replaced by a
  voltage source of that value (the inductor by a current source), and solve that resistive circuit for $x$.
* Only $v_C$ and $i_L$ are guaranteed continuous. A resistor's voltage, a capacitor's current, or an
  inductor's voltage can all jump at $t = 0$.
* Find $\tau$ from the circuit **after** the switch moves. If the switch changes the circuit's
  topology, the time constant changes too.
* If the switch moves at $t_0$ instead of 0, replace $t$ by $t - t_0$ in the exponential.

> **Why is $\tau$ the same everywhere?** A first-order circuit has one state variable. Every other voltage
> and current is a fixed combination of that state and the (constant) sources. So they all decay with that
> state's single exponential, only with different starting and ending values.

steps.title: Example
steps.md: The capacitor has been discharged through the 4 kΩ for a long time, so $v_C(0^-) = 0$. The switch closes at $t = 0$.

q.name: A3
q.prompt: What is the final value $v_C(\infty)$?
q.why: With the capacitor open, it's a divider: $\frac{4}{2 + 4} \cdot 12 = 8$ V.

q.name: A4
q.prompt: What is the time constant $\tau$ for $t > 0$?
q.why: Kill the 12 V source (short). The capacitor sees $2\text{k} \parallel 4\text{k} = \tfrac43$ kΩ, so $\tau = \tfrac43\text{ k}\Omega \cdot 1\ \mu\text{F} = \tfrac43$ ms.

q.name: A5
q.prompt: What is $v_C$ at $t = \tau$?

q.name: A6
q.prompt: Now track the voltage across the 2 kΩ resistor, $v_{R1}$. What is $v_{R1}(0^+)$?
q.why: At $0^+$ the capacitor is still at 0 V, so the whole 12 V appears across the 2 kΩ. Unlike $v_C$, a resistor voltage *can* jump.

q.name: A7
q.prompt: What is $v_{R1}(\infty)$?
q.why: $12 - v_C(\infty) = 12 - 8 = 4$ V. So $v_{R1}(t) = 4 + 8e^{-t/\tau}$, with the same $\tau$ as $v_C$.

steps.title: Sketch it before you calculate
steps.md:
Once you have the three numbers, you can sketch any waveform in seconds:

1. Mark $x(0^+)$ on the vertical axis and draw a dashed line at $x(\infty)$.
2. Draw the initial slope: a straight line from $x(0^+)$ that would reach $x(\infty)$ at $t = \tau$.
3. Curve away from that line so you're 63% of the way there at $\tau$, 86% at $2\tau$ and 95% at $3\tau$.

In the example, $v_C$ rises from 0 toward 8 V, while $v_{R1}$ falls from 12 V toward 4 V, both with
$\tau = 4/3$ ms. At every instant they add to 12 V, as KVL requires. That's a quick check of your sketch.

> **Watch out:** a first-order waveform moves *monotonically* from $x(0^+)$ to $x(\infty)$. It never overshoots
> or oscillates. If your sketch wiggles, something is wrong. (Oscillation needs two energy-storage
> elements, which is the topic of the RLC units.)

q.name: Q1
q.prompt: Quiz: a capacitor starts at 10 V and relaxes toward a Thévenin voltage of 2 V. What is its voltage after one time constant?

q.name: Q2
q.prompt: Quiz: a 6 V source drives an inductor through a 3 Ω resistor. What is the inductor current in DC steady state?
q.why: The inductor is a short in steady state, so $i = 6/3 = 2$ A.

q.name: Q3
q.prompt: Quiz: in the example, what current flows through the 4 kΩ resistor right after the switch closes?
q.why: It's in parallel with the capacitor, which is still at $v_C(0^+) = 0$ V. So it carries no current at $0^+$. All 6 mA from the 2 kΩ goes into the capacitor.

unit.title: Step and impulse responses
unit.intro:
Describe inputs with the unit step and the impulse. The impulse response shows a circuit's
natural behavior and, through convolution, gives its response to any input.

steps.title: The unit step
steps.md: The **unit step** $u(t)$ is 0 for $t < 0$ and 1 for $t > 0$. Writing $v_i = V_0\,u(t)$ is a compact way to say "a source of $V_0$ switched on at $t = 0$". With $v_C(0^-) = 0$, the recipe gives $$v_C(t) = V_0\left(1 - e^{-t/RC}\right)u(t), \qquad v_R(t) = V_0\,e^{-t/RC}\,u(t).$$ This is the circuit's **step response**.

q.name: A1
q.prompt: A 5 V step drives the RC circuit with the capacitor initially uncharged. What is $v_R(0^+)$?
q.why: $v_C(0^+) = 0$, so the whole step appears across $R$ at first, then decays as $5e^{-t/RC}$.

steps.title: Building signals from steps
steps.md:
Steps are building blocks. A **rectangular pulse** of height $V_0$ from $t = 0$ to $t = T$ is a step up
followed by a step down:

$$x(t) = V_0\,u(t) - V_0\,u(t - T).$$

Because the circuit is linear and **time-invariant** (delaying the input just delays the output), its
response is the step response minus a delayed copy:

* For $0 < t < T$: $v_C = V_0\left(1 - e^{-t/\tau}\right)$, charging.
* For $t > T$: the input is back to zero, so $v_C$ decays from its value at $T$: $v_C(T)\,e^{-(t-T)/\tau}$.

> **Intuition:** a short pulse ($T \ll \tau$) barely charges the capacitor before it ends. A long pulse
> ($T \gg \tau$) lets it fully charge, so the output looks like a copy of the input with rounded edges. The
> ratio $T/\tau$ decides which regime you're in.

q.name: A1b
q.prompt: A 5 V pulse lasting exactly one time constant ($T = \tau$) drives the RC circuit from rest. What is $v_C$ when the pulse ends?
q.why: During the pulse it's the step response, so $v_C(\tau) = 5(1 - e^{-1}) \approx 3.16$ V. After that it decays toward 0 with the same $\tau$.

steps.title: The impulse
steps.md:
Take a pulse of height $1/x$ and width $x$. Its area is 1 no matter what $x$ is. In the limit $x \to 0$ it
becomes the **unit impulse** $\delta(t)$: infinitely tall, infinitely short, with area 1. An impulse of area
$A$ is written $A\,\delta(t)$.

The running integral of $\delta$ is the step, $\int_{-\infty}^t \delta(\tau)\,d\tau = u(t)$, so
$\delta(t) = \dfrac{du}{dt}$.

**Units.** Since $\delta(t)$ has area 1 over time, $\delta(t)$ itself has units of 1/s. A voltage impulse
$A\,\delta(t)$ therefore has its strength $A$ in **volt-seconds**, and a current impulse has its strength in
ampere-seconds, which are coulombs. That's a useful reminder that a current impulse simply delivers a
fixed packet of charge.

**The sifting property.** Multiplying by an impulse and integrating picks out one value:
$\int x(\alpha)\,\delta(t - \alpha)\,d\alpha = x(t)$. This is what makes convolution work.

> **Intuition:** an impulse is an idealized "kick": a hammer blow, a camera flash, a lightning strike.
> It's over before the system can react, so all that matters is *how much* total push it delivered (its area).

steps.title: An impulse into an RC circuit
steps.md:
Drive the RC circuit with $v_i = A\,\delta(t)$. During the pulse the source is huge compared with $v_C$,
so $i_C \approx \frac{A}{xR}$ for the pulse width $x$. The charge delivered is $Q = A/R$, so the
capacitor voltage **jumps**:

$$v_C(0^+) = \frac{Q}{C} = \frac{A}{RC}.$$

(This is the one case where a capacitor's voltage can change instantly, because the current really
is infinite for an instant.) After that the input is zero, and the capacitor just decays naturally:

$$v_C(t) = \frac{A}{RC}\,e^{-t/RC}\,u(t).$$

So an impulse simply **sets an initial condition**, then lets you watch the natural response.

q.name: A2
q.prompt: An impulse of area 2 mV·s drives an RC circuit with $R = 1$ kΩ and $C = 1$ µF. What is $v_C(0^+)$?

q.name: A3
q.prompt: How much charge did that impulse deliver to the capacitor?

steps.title: Why impulses matter
steps.md:
1. **Short pulses act like impulses.** Any pulse much shorter than the circuit's time constants gives
   nearly the impulse response, scaled by the pulse's **area**. Its shape doesn't matter.
2. **The impulse response $h(t)$ reveals the natural response**, which you need for initial conditions,
   steps and everything else.
3. **It predicts the response to any input.** Write an input $x(t)$ as a sum of narrow pulses, each of
   area $x(\alpha)\,\Delta\alpha$. By linearity and time invariance, each one produces a scaled, shifted
   copy of $h$. Adding them up gives the **convolution integral**

$$y(t) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(\alpha)\,h(t - \alpha)\,d\alpha = x(t) * h(t).$$

**Reading the convolution integral.** The output *now* (time $t$) is a weighted sum of all past inputs.
The input from time $\alpha$ is weighted by $h(t - \alpha)$, the impulse response evaluated at "how long
ago" that input happened. For the RC circuit, $h(t) = \frac{1}{RC}e^{-t/RC}u(t)$, so:

* recent inputs count the most, and inputs from long ago (many $\tau$) are almost forgotten;
* inputs from the future count for nothing, since $h = 0$ for negative times. The circuit is **causal**.

> **Intuition:** the RC circuit has a fading memory, like a moving average that weights recent values
> more. That is why it smooths a noisy signal, and it is your first glimpse of a **low-pass filter**,
> which you will study in the frequency-response units.

q.name: A4
q.prompt: A 10 V pulse lasting 1 µs drives an RC circuit with $RC = 1$ ms (capacitor initially empty). About what voltage is the capacitor left at?
q.why: The pulse is 1000× shorter than $\tau$, so treat it as an impulse of area $10 \times 10^{-6}$ V·s. Then $v_C \approx A/(RC) = 10^{-5}/10^{-3} = 10$ mV.

q.name: A5
q.prompt: For a pulse much shorter than the time constant, which property of the pulse sets the response?
q.why: Only the area (the integral of the input) matters in the short-pulse limit. A tall thin pulse and a short triangle of the same area give the same result.

q.name: Q1
q.prompt: Quiz: an impulse of area 3 mV·s drives an RC circuit with $RC = 0.5$ ms. What is $v_C(0^+)$?

q.name: Q2
q.prompt: Quiz: in that same circuit, what is $v_C$ at $t = 1$ ms?

q.name: Q3
q.prompt: Quiz: how can you get a linear circuit's impulse response from its step response?
q.why: $\delta = du/dt$, and linear time-invariant circuits commute with differentiation. For the RC: $\frac{d}{dt}(1 - e^{-t/RC}) = \frac1{RC}e^{-t/RC}$, matching $A/(RC)\,e^{-t/RC}$ with $A = 1$.
